title: HINTS Exam — Central vs Peripheral Vertigo

summary: HINTS is a three-part bedside exam that, in skilled hands, outperforms early MRI for catching a posterior circulation stroke masquerading as vertigo — but it only applies to continuous acute vestibular syndrome, and a NORMAL head impulse test is the worrisome finding, the opposite of what intuition suggests.
whyThisMatters: Posterior circulation strokes can present as isolated vertigo with a benign-looking general neuro exam, and this is one of the classic 'stroke masquerading as something benign' presentations — HINTS exists specifically to catch this subset before a normal CT or even a falsely-negative early MRI provides false reassurance, but only when applied to the right patient population and performed with genuine skill.
clinicalTakeaway:
Apply HINTS only to ACUTE VESTIBULAR SYNDROME — continuous vertigo/nausea/unsteadiness lasting more than 24 hours with nystagmus, NOT episodic positional vertigo (which needs Dix-Hallpike instead).

The three components:
- Head Impulse: a NORMAL result — no catch-up saccade — is the WORRISOME finding suggesting a central cause, since an abnormal/positive result with a catch-up saccade actually suggests a peripheral cause.
- Nystagmus direction: unidirectional nystagmus suggests peripheral, direction-changing suggests central.
- Test of Skew: any vertical misalignment on alternate cover testing is always suspicious for a central cause.

Remember this by INFARCT: Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test — that pattern flags a likely central/stroke cause.

This is a genuinely skill-dependent exam — know your own comfort level and don't over-trust a HINTS exam performed without real training, and maintain a lower threshold for imaging/neurology involvement if you're not confident in your own findings.

body.text: Who this applies to — acute vestibular syndrome only

HINTS is validated ONLY for ACUTE VESTIBULAR SYNDROME — continuous vertigo, nausea, and unsteadiness lasting more than 24 hours, typically with nystagmus present at rest. Do NOT apply it to episodic/positional vertigo (brief spells lasting seconds to minutes, classically triggered by position change, the BPPV pattern) — that population needs a different bedside exam entirely (Dix-Hallpike maneuver), and applying HINTS logic to episodic vertigo is a category error that can mislead rather than clarify.

rows: Rapidly rotate the patient's head a small amount to one side while they fixate on your nose/a target; watch for a corrective 'catch-up' saccade after the movement

A NORMAL result (NO catch-up saccade — eyes stay locked on target) is the WORRISOME finding, suggesting the vestibulo-ocular reflex pathway isn't the problem, which points toward a CENTRAL cause. An ABNORMAL result (a visible catch-up saccade) actually suggests a PERIPHERAL cause (the reflex itself is impaired, as expected with a peripheral vestibular lesion)
Observe the direction/pattern of spontaneous nystagmus in different gaze positions
UNIDIRECTIONAL nystagmus (same direction regardless of gaze direction) suggests PERIPHERAL. Direction-CHANGING nystagmus (different direction on different gaze positions) suggests CENTRAL
Alternate cover-uncover test between the two eyes, watching for a vertical corrective refixation movement
ANY vertical misalignment/skew deviation is ALWAYS suspicious for a CENTRAL cause — this is a specific, high-value sign

body.text: Mnemonic: INFARCT — Impulse Normal, Fast-phase Alternating (direction-changing nystagmus), Refixation on Cover Test (a positive skew test) — this combination of findings points toward a central/stroke cause, the pattern you don't want to miss.
Diagnostic performance — and its real caveat

In the hands of a trained examiner, HINTS has been reported with sensitivity approaching 100% and specificity around 90-94% for detecting a central (stroke) cause in acute vestibular syndrome — genuinely outperforming early MRI (which can be falsely negative for a small posterior fossa stroke in the first 24-48 hours).

This is a real and clinically important finding, but it comes with an important caveat: this level of accuracy was demonstrated by examiners with specific neuro-otologic training and experience.

The exam is genuinely operator-dependent, and a HINTS exam performed by someone without real training/practice in the technique should not be trusted with the same confidence as the literature's reported performance.

Know your own comfort level with this exam. If you're not confident in your HINTS findings, or the overall clinical picture still concerns you despite a reassuring exam, maintain a lower threshold for neuroimaging and neurology involvement — HINTS is a powerful tool in skilled hands, not a substitute for clinical judgment when your own skill/confidence with the technique is limited.
